findings: A: STRONG. Argued at full strength - the option reuses the contract's own vocabulary ('the booked minute'), and the passage is saturated with central-tendency figures (median crossing twenty-four minutes, median barrier-to-ramp thirty-nine to fifty-four), which primes a reader to hear the payment test as an average. Dies on 'at least ninety-two per cent of its sailings berth within ten minutes of the booked minute': the test is the share of sailings inside a fixed window, not the mean lateness. Supported limb = the booked minute and the ten-minute window; refused limb = 'the average sailing'. Teaches the proportion-vs-mean confusion, a real metric misconception.

B: MODERATE. Argued at full strength - the piece puts the clause and the withdrawal in one causal frame (Bexwarden 'does not accept that it caused any of this'), so a reader holding the events but not the dates can fuse them, and the one-boat era is a natural-sounding trigger for writing a punctuality clause. Dies on two dated spans: 'Since 2011 the operator has earned a quality payment' and 'Alison Bexwarden drafted the punctuality clause for the transport authority in 2011' against 'in 2016 the relief boat's passenger certificate ran out'. Clause precedes withdrawal by five years. Supported limb = the clause entered the contract at a datable moment; refused limb = that the moment was the withdrawal.

D: STRONGEST on the sheet. Argued at full strength - the passage explicitly connects cancellations to the metric AND flags them as the thing Bexwarden would change, so a reader who registers 'cancellations are handled wrongly here' and then guesses the mechanism will very plausibly guess a partial penalty; 'reduced, though not withdrawn' is exactly the proportionate design a regulator would write, and it is consistent with a naive reading in which a cancelled sailing counts against the ninety-two per cent. Dies twice: 'A sailing that does not run is not late; it leaves the count altogether' inverts the direction, and the worked example settles the sign - 'the crossing lost forty-one sailings to weather and a gearbox, and its reliability figure was ninety-seven per cent, the highest it had ever been'. Supported limb = cancellations do interact with the metric and Bexwarden does object; refused limb = the direction of the interaction.

C (KEY) ARITHMETIC CONFIRMED: 'has taken it in twenty-three of the last twenty-four quarters' gives 24-23 = 1 unpaid quarter, and 24 quarters = 72 months = exactly six years, so 'unpaid in one quarter during the past six years' is precisely true with nothing rounded or approximated.

C (KEY) REWORDING CONFIRMED SOUND: the change from 'one quarter OF the past six years' to 'one quarter DURING the past six years' removes a live ambiguity. 'One quarter of the past six years' admits a fraction reading (a quarter of six years = eighteen months), under which the option would be false; 'during' forces the calendar-quarter reading, under which it is exactly true. The repair fixes a genuine defect rather than churning bytes.
justification: All three distractors pair a text-supported limb with a text-refused limb and each dies on a citable span; none is defensible as a second key. The key's arithmetic reconciles exactly (24 quarters, 23 taken, 1 missed, 72 months = 6 years) and the 'of' to 'during' rewording closes a fraction-reading ambiguity that would otherwise have made the key false on one parse. Pass.

findings: B: MODERATE-STRONG. Argued at full strength - seventy is a real number Cottam himself utters, and it sits two sentences from the old book inside a single quotation, so a skimmer can bind the salient figure to the salient topic. 'As they still do' borrows plausibility from 'The water is the same width it always was', which primes a nothing-really-changed reading. Dies on the quotation read in order: 'Two boats and the old book gave you a departure every twenty-five minutes... One boat gives you one every seventy' assigns seventy to the present, twenty-five to 2005; and 'the interval between departures went from twenty-five minutes to thirty-two' refutes 'as they still do'. Supported limb = seventy is a real interval Cottam names; refused limb = its date and the continuity claim.

C: MODERATE. Argued at full strength - the reader has correctly absorbed that the old book under-allowed for something, which is Cottam's actual thesis, and loading is the most available candidate for an under-allowance on a vehicle ferry; the passage even supplies a berthing-procedure duration to lend the idea texture. Dies twice: the passage contains no 2005 loading claim at all, and the direction is inverted by 'The linkspan ... was rebuilt in 2013 for heavier axle loads, and its locking sequence takes a manufacturer's ninety seconds at each berth', which Cottam files under 'work that really has got longer' - longer NOW, not 'longer then than it does now'. Supported limb = the old book under-allowed for something; refused limb = the identity of that something and the direction of change.

D: STRONG. Argued at full strength - genuinely tempting, because Cottam's 'the old seventy-one per cent measured a promise nobody could keep' can be heard as a retrospective judgement rather than a contemporaneous figure, and because the contractual regime demonstrably begins in 2011, six years after the book, which invites the inference that measurement began then too. It also fits the article's arc of a naive old book later disciplined by metrics. Dies on 'The published reliability figure stood at seventy-one per cent in 2005' - a published 2005 figure IS measurement of how late the boat was. Supported limb = the contractual payment regime postdates 2005; refused limb = that measurement as such did.

A (KEY) VERIFIED: 'The median crossing that year took twenty-four minutes against an eighteen-minute booking' plus 'six of the nine added minutes only brought the book level with the boat' - the 2005 book allowed eighteen against an actual twenty-four, uniquely supporting A.
justification: Each distractor is built on a real inference a careful-but-hurried reader makes, and each dies on one span rather than on vagueness. D is the best-constructed of the three because it fails only on a single dated figure while every other element of its reasoning is sound. No distractor is defensible against the key. Pass.

findings: A: MODERATE. Argued at full strength - the chronology is deliberately scattered across paragraphs one, three and five, and a reader anchored on 'In 2005 the crossing ... was printed as eighteen minutes. This year it is printed as twenty-seven' without the intermediate date can read the padding as a recent response to a one-boat service, which is a coherent operational story in its own right. Dies on 'The book went from eighteen minutes to twenty-four in 2013, three years before the certificate ran out' - the interval is spelled out explicitly. Supported limb = both events happened; refused limb = their order.

B: MODERATE. Argued at full strength - the linkspan rebuild and the certificate lapse sit one sentence apart in the same paragraph, and a reader can construct a real-sounding causal bridge: a linkspan 'rebuilt in 2013 for heavier axle loads' is the kind of change that can render an older vessel non-compliant, so the certificate becomes the paperwork symptom of the rebuild. The article's general posture, that official reasons conceal operational ones, encourages exactly this move. Dies for want of any linking span: the text gives one reason and only one - 'in 2016 the relief boat's passenger certificate ran out and the company did not replace her' - and it is a PASSENGER certificate, while the linkspan enters the text for a different purpose (its ninety-second locking sequence as added crossing time). The comparative 'more to do with' demands evidence the text never supplies. Supported limb = both facts exist and are adjacent; refused limb = any causal relation between them.

C: STRONGEST on this item, and the one the stem is really testing. Argued at full strength - Cottam's own words make the boat the whole of the frequency story: 'Two boats and the old book gave you a departure every twenty-five minutes... One boat gives you one every seventy. Pad the book by nothing at all and you'd still have that.' A reader who takes the named operations director at his word concludes the boat began it. Dies on the writer's deliberate correction in the closing paragraph: 'the interval between departures went from twenty-five minutes to thirty-two' before the certificate lapsed, glossed as 'Some of the frequency was gone before the boat was.' Note the quality of this construction - it dies not on a misreading but on the writer's qualification of a source's overstatement, which is precisely what 'implied' in the stem asks the student to catch. Supported limb = the boat is the dominant frequency cause; refused limb = that it was the first.

D (KEY) VERIFIED, and note the C/D contrast is well engineered: the text supplies the MAGNITUDE (25->32 attributable to the book change, 32->70 once the boat had gone, plus Cottam's 'Pad the book by nothing at all and you'd still have that') while explicitly denying the PRIMACY. D claims magnitude and survives; C claims primacy and dies. The pair is discriminated by the text, not by taste.
justification: Three distractors, three distinct citable kills, and the C/D pair is separated by an explicit textual denial rather than by a judgement call. C is a model distractor: it fails only because the writer corrects the source who states it. Pass.

findings: A: MODERATE. Argued at full strength - the closing paragraph is corrosive in aggregate ('Where Cattermay's case thins is the join'; 'she says herself that she cannot pull them apart'; 'the stamps would bear either of the other two just as well'), so a reader who registers the tone can over-extend the scepticism to the numbers; and A's second clause is exactly right, which lends its first clause borrowed credibility. Dies on 'Nobody disputes the stamps. Cottam has accepted the barrier series in writing, and does not contest the fifteen minutes', reinforced by her unchallenged 'The fifteen minutes are real, and I'd stand behind them in any room.' Supported limb = the explanation is doubted; refused limb = that the minutes are.

C: STRONGEST on the sheet, and the closest thing to a defensible second key anywhere in this unit - examined and rejected. Argued at full strength - C reproduces Cattermay's own hedge almost verbatim in substance ('Ask me how many of them the timetable put there and I'll give you a range, not a number' IS 'at fault, though not by how much'), and the piece's title and opening image, a mate reading a paperback at the slip because the boat is booked to sit there, both point at the timetable. A reader who takes the source's self-description as the writer's verdict lands here honestly. Dies on 'The timetable is the reading she prefers; the stamps would bear either of the other two just as well' - that withholds the fault itself, not merely its size: the timetable is one of three readings the same evidence would carry equally, so nothing has been shown. The whole item turns on 'we do not know HOW MUCH' (C) versus 'we do not know WHETHER' (the text), and the text is unambiguous. Not defensible.

D: MODERATE. Argued at full strength - a clean inversion, tempting for a reader who retains that the paragraph contains one concession and one doubt but not which attaches to which; both halves have isolated textual material behind them, since the piece does contain doubt and does present the timetable thesis sympathetically for two paragraphs before correcting it. Dies on both limbs: 'Nobody disputes the stamps' refuses the doubt about numbers, and 'the stamps would bear either of the other two just as well' refuses the grant about the timetable. Weakest of the three because it fails twice, but it is the necessary fourth cell of the 2x2 and it teaches the limb-swap error.

B (KEY) VERIFIED: 'Nobody disputes the stamps' gives acceptance of the numbers, 'Where Cattermay's case thins is the join' gives refusal of the cause. The four options form a complete 2x2 over the two axes, which is why no option is redundant and why the sheet gives no form advantage here.
justification: The 2x2 construction means each distractor teaches a distinct, nameable error - over-extended scepticism (A), fault-established-but-unquantified (C), limb swap (D). C was tested hard as a possible second key and fails on an explicit span; the others fail decisively. Pass.

findings: A (REWRITTEN): well-formed. Supported limb, and unusually strong - 'In 2005 the crossing to the north shore was printed as eighteen minutes. This year it is printed as twenty-seven' (booked slower) with 'The published reliability figure stood at seventy-one per cent in 2005. Last year it was ninety-six' (runs to time more often). That first limb names the article's central paradox correctly, which is what gives the option its pull. Refused limb: 'the passengers who were not consulted' dies on 'In the consultation that preceded it, sixty-one per cent of those answering ranked getting across sooner below knowing when the boat would go.' The consultation happened, respondents answered, and their preference is on the record - and it is the load-bearing fact of Bexwarden's defence, 'The clause measures what people asked to have measured.' The option asserts a grievance the text specifically forecloses. One span, decisive.

B (REWRITTEN): well-formed, and pedagogically the best of the three. Supported limb: the two datasets genuinely do tell opposite stories - 'By the only measure the contract knows, the crossing has never run better' against 'The median time from barrier to far ramp has gone from thirty-nine minutes to fifty-four.' Refused limb: 'a dispute over which of them to believe' dies on 'Nobody disputes the stamps. Cottam has accepted the barrier series in writing, and does not contest the fifteen minutes.' Both figures are accepted by every party; the disagreement sits downstream of the data, on causation, not on credibility. The repair to B's previously face-invalid limb has landed - its first limb is now fully supported, so the option is refutable only on its second limb, which is the correct construction for a main-idea distractor.

C (RESHAPED): well-formed. Supported limb: the clause is real, current, drafted by a named source, and a genuine strand - 'Since 2011 the operator has earned a quality payment in any quarter when at least ninety-two per cent of its sailings berth within ten minutes of the booked minute.' Refused limb: 'the argument over whether it should go into the next one unchanged' dies on THREE independent spans - 'None of the three is arguing about the sentence Bexwarden raised herself'; Bexwarden's own 'That's the line I'd change ... and nobody writes to me about it'; and 'The draft that went to the harbour board in July carries the 2011 clause word for word, including the line about cancelled sailings.' The absence of that argument is the article's closing irony, so C asserts the exact opposite of the ending. The reshape to a noun phrase also makes C structurally parallel with A, B and D.

STRUCTURE: all three rewritten distractors now follow the same correct pattern - a first limb the text fully supports, a second limb the text flatly contradicts on a citable span. None of the three fails on emphasis or scope alone, which is a stronger construction than dying on 'too narrow'. C would additionally fail on scope (one strand of four) but does not need that argument.

NO SECOND KEY: each of A, B and C was argued at full strength and each is refuted by direct textual contradiction, not by preference. D is uniquely supported on both limbs - punctuality up (71 to 96 per cent), journeys longer (39 to 54 minutes), and three named parties assigning the gap to different causes (Cattermay to the timetable, Cottam to the boat, Bexwarden refusing the clause). D does not overclaim.

CROSS-REFERENCE TO G-STEM: because all three distractors now sit off the causal axis, the passage-blind topic-coherence route noted at G-STEM becomes the binding constraint on this item. That is the accepted structural floor for a main-idea key and is recorded there, not treated as a distractor defect here.
justification: The three rewritten distractors are each better built than what they replaced: every one pairs a genuinely supported limb with a limb the passage refuses outright, and every refusal cites a specific span - one for A, one for B, three for C. None is defensible as a second key under full-strength argument. Pass.
